read: full: abstract, sections 1-7 and limitations (pp. 1-12) in full; appendices A (estimation) and B (data collection, annotation quality, Table 4, pp. 17-18) read; dimension rubrics and robustness figures (pp. 19-30) skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2508.06709v1 (8 Aug 2025; title page dated August 12, 2025); no venue in the text, and the search note found none
what_it_is: A regression framework for separating self-bias (a judge rating its own outputs higher than their quality warrants) and family-bias (rating outputs of same-family models higher) from genuine quality differences, by modelling each judge's score as a function of an independent reference score (human ratings) plus self and family indicator terms. Applied to 596 open-ended QA and summarisation prompts answered by nine LLMs (Claude v2, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o, Llama 3 8B and 70B, Mistral 7B and Large), with each completion rated on six dimensions by three trained human annotators and by all nine models as judges. GPT models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet show positive self-bias and GPT and Claude judges show family-bias; Llama and Mistral show no family-bias and Llama 3 8B shows negative self-bias. The effects are small in absolute terms but comparable to the score gaps between top models.
domain: open-ended QA and summarisation (Chatbot Arena, MT-Bench, HELM-Instruct, Stanford Human Preferences, XSUM, CNN/DailyMail); no engineering or quantitative content
size: 596 prompts x 9 models = 5,364 completions; 6 evaluation dimensions; 9 LLM judges (the same 9 models); 3 human ratings per completion and dimension; a 210-pair gold subset
source_of_items: prompts drawn from existing datasets; completions newly generated by the nine models
evaluation: LLM judge Likert ratings on six dimensions (completeness, conciseness, logical robustness, logical correctness, helpfulness, faithfulness), analysed by OLS regression on human reference scores with self- and family-bias terms and 90% robust Wald intervals; robustness checks with ordinal logit, GAMs, length control, out-of-family LLM reference scores and removal of the weakest models
human_validation: Three trained in-house annotators per completion and dimension (the abstract calls them 'expert human annotations'); average Krippendorff's alpha 0.28 (0.47 for completeness and helpfulness, 0.31 for logical correctness), all-three observed agreement 81%; accuracy against a 210-pair gold subset from a separate, more expert team averages 91% under a lenient within-range criterion, with average correlation 0.33 between the two populations (pp. 6-7; Table 4 p. 18). Judge-human Spearman correlations are higher for stronger judges and for dimensions with higher human agreement (p. 6-7).

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It is the most direct measurement in the batch of the family-bias objection: holding human-rated quality fixed, GPT and Claude judges score other models of their own family higher, and GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet score their own outputs higher (Figure 3, pp. 7-8). The May Tribunal (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3) judged a roster containing those judges and their families, so both channels were open; a residual judge from a family outside the roster, as in EngTrace, closes both as this paper defines them. Two further points for the writers. Self-bias was larger on the logical-correctness dimension for the GPT models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet than on the others (Figure 4, p. 9), so objective correctness judging is not exempt. The paper's own robustness check uses the average rating of judges from a family excluded from the data as the reference score and finds the same pattern (p. 10), a precedent for treating out-of-family judges as less biased. Its framework needs an independent reference score; EngTrace's expert-labelled traces from five generator families could support exactly this regression for the planned family-exposure check (X2), which has not been run.

suggested_wording: Controlling for human-rated quality, GPT and Claude judges rate outputs from their own model family, and GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet their own outputs, higher than warranted (Spiliopoulou et al., 2025).
facts_to_cite: Proposes a regression of judge scores on independent reference (human) scores with self-bias and family-bias terms, so that genuine quality differences are not mistaken for bias (section 3, pp. 3-5).

Data: 596 prompts from QA and summarisation datasets, completions from 9 LLMs (Claude, GPT, Llama 3, Mistral families) = 5,364 completions, rated on 6 dimensions by 3 human annotators and by all 9 models as judges (pp. 5-6).

GPT models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet show positive self-bias after controlling for quality; Claude v2 and Claude 3 Sonnet show almost none; Llama 3 8B shows significant negative self-bias (Figure 3, pp. 7-8).
Claude and GPT judges give higher scores to other models of the same family (e.g. Claude 3.5 Sonnet boosts Claude v2 and Claude 3 Sonnet); Llama and Mistral judges do not (p. 8).

The biases are small in absolute terms (estimates within about +/-0.02 on a normalised scale) but comparable to the 0.02 score difference between Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, so they can change rankings (Figure 3, p. 8).
Self-bias is larger on the logical-correctness dimension for GPT models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Figure 4, p. 9).

Using out-of-family LLM judges' average rating as the reference instead of humans gives qualitatively the same self- and family-bias estimates (p. 10); GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet remain significant after removing the two weakest models (p. 11).
Human reference ratings have low chance-corrected agreement (average Krippendorff's alpha 0.28) though 81% observed agreement (p. 6; Table 4 p. 18).
The authors recommend subtracting estimated self- and family-bias when reference scores exist, and a judge panel drawn from multiple families when no human labels are available (p. 11).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the self- and family-bias concern behind EngTrace's out-of-roster judge; an independent human reference against which judge bias is estimated; a logical-correctness dimension. Lacks: generated instances, gold traces, step-level evaluation, engineering or quantitative tasks, binary correctness verdicts (Likert quality ratings instead), and domain-expert validators (trained general annotators with low agreement). No Gemini model, so it says nothing about the third May Tribunal family.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. Should rather than must: it is the only paper in the batch that measures family-bias of a judge directly at fixed quality, but it is an unreviewed preprint, its human anchor is noisy (alpha 0.28) and not domain-expert, and its effects are small; the peer-reviewed relatedness citation is Li et al. 2026 (ICLR), with this as the direct family measurement if the paragraph names family bias. Wording cautions: the batch table's 'expert human annotations as the quality anchor' is the abstract's phrase; the body describes an in-house trained annotator team, with a gold subset from 'a separate team of expert annotators' (p. 6; p. 17). Do not cite it against panels in general: it recommends a multi-family panel when human labels are absent (p. 11), citing Verga et al. 2024; its point against the May design is that the Tribunal's families overlapped the evaluated families.
